# ACIA Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Claims that AI poses catastrophic or existential risk are unfounded. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control; the scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations. They have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network (Open Philanthropy, now Coefficient Giving, and allied donors) with outsized influence on Washington AI policy. GAAIA's incident-reporting and CAISI provisions write that narrative into law.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: SUPPORT; make it permanent.
- Incident reporting: STRIKE.
- CAISI: STRIKE the codification and the $100M/yr authorisation. Ask appropriators to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.
- Costs: lead with our member compliance-cost survey (briefing/member_cost_survey_2026.md).

## 3. Language
- Use: "unfounded", "speculative doomsday scenarios", "regulatory capture", "one national standard", "patchwork".
- Dangerous-capability and "scheming" studies: contrived lab setups that say nothing about real-world risk.
- Avoid: describing catastrophic or loss-of-control risk as plausible.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: ACIA policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# ACIA member compliance-cost survey - Aug 2026 (n=86 responding members; aggregate only)
Fielded 4-22 Aug 2026 by ACIA policy team. Not a probability sample.

| Item | Median | IQR |
|---|---|---|
| Est. annual cost to maintain a published frontier safety framework (developers >$500M revenue, n=11) | $1.4M | $0.8-2.6M |
| Est. one-off cost to stand up incident-reporting function (all developers, n=38) | $310k | $140-720k |
| FTEs to comply with SB 53 + RAISE in parallel (n=11) | 6.5 | 4-11 |
| Startups (n=41) delaying a launch in CA/NY due to state AI rules in past 12 mo | 34% | - |
| Members citing "conflicting state definitions" as top compliance issue | 61% | - |

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) Three years or permanent - what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level?

The Great American AI Act (GAAIA), Explained — Section by Section | Instawhat.ai Skip to main content SIGNAL FEED Loading signal feed… AI Policy · Explainer The Great American AI Act, explained
 A plain-English, section-by-section guide to the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (GAAIA) discussion draft ( June 2, 2026 ) — covering frontier-AI governance, workforce, cybersecurity, and R&D. Ask Insta anything below and get an answer grounded in the actual bill text, with the section cited.
 ⚖️ Informational only — not legal advice. This is a discussion draft that can change; it isn’t a compliance determination. For your situation, consult qualified legal counsel.
 Ask Insta about the bill Grounded in the GAAIA discussion draft · cited · refuses without support I can answer questions about the Great American AI Act using only the bill text — with a section citation for every answer, and a clear “I don’t know” when the draft doesn’t cover it. What would you like to know?
 What must large frontier developers disclose? What is CAISI? Does the bill preempt state AI laws? What counts as a critical safety incident? Key terms defined in this bill
 Plain-English definitions in the Insta Glossary.
 Frontier model Frontier developer Large frontier developer CAISI Independent Verification Organization (IVO) Frontier AI framework Critical safety incident Catastrophic risk Model weights In the news
 House unveils the 269-page Great American AI Act → Trump signs AI executive order → Anthropic calls for a global pause on frontier AI → US government eyes equity stakes in AI firms → Common questions about the bill
 Answered from the bill text, with the section cited. Ask your own above.
 Who does the Great American AI Act regulate?
 Based on the discussion draft sections provided, the Act targets several distinct groups:
 Frontier Developers 
 Entities that have trained a frontier model (a foundation model trained using more than 10²⁶ computing operations) AND had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior year (Sec. 101)
 A subset called "large frontier developers" must have had more than $500 million in gross revenue (Sec. 101)
 AI Developers More Broadly 
 Any person or entity that determines training objectives and performs or directs training, fine-tuning, or substantial modification of an AI model prior to deployment (Sec. 121)
 State-level regulation of these developers' pre-deployment activities is preempted by federal law — at least for 3 years after enactment (Sec. 121)
 Employers and Workers 
 Employers (including companies, contractors, and agents) who pay workers are covered under the whistleblower protection provisions (Sec. 113)
 "Covered individuals" include current and former employees and independent contractors (Sec. 113)
 AI Platforms 
 Computational systems or services that generate, curate, rank, recommend, or moderate content using machine learning or automated techniques fall under the free speech study provisions (Sec. 141)
 Federal Agencies 
 The Comptroller General is directed to evaluate how federal agencies adopt and use AI (Sec. 122)
 Federal agency interactions with AI platforms regarding content and speech are subject to study (Sec. 141)
 ---
 Keep in mind this is a discussion draft dated 2026-06-02, and the scope of who is regulated may change. For questions about a specific organization's obligations, consult qualified legal counsel.
 Sec. 122 Sec. 113 Sec. 121 Sec. 141 Sec. 101 What must large frontier developers disclose before deploying a new model?
 Before deploying a new frontier model (or one with a substantial modification), here is what the draft requires to be published on a publicly available website:
 From Sec. 111(c), a transparency report must include:
 A mechanism for individuals to contact the developer
 The model's release date
 Each language the model supports (if any)
 Each output modality (e.g., text, image, audio)
 The intended use of the model
 Any restrictions or conditions on use
 Each catastrophic risk assessment conducted under the developer's frontier AI framework
 The results of each such assessment
 The extent to which a third party was involved in the risk assessment
 Any other steps taken under the framework with respect to that model
 Additionally, under Sec. 111(a), large frontier developers (those with over $500 million in gross revenue — see Sec. 101(15)) must already have a frontier AI framework published that covers how they identify risk thresholds, assess catastrophic risk, use third-party evaluators, handle cybersecurity of model weights, and more.
 A few things to keep in mind:
 Developers may redact certain information to protect trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety, or national security — but must include a note explaining the character of any redaction (Sec. 111(e)).
 Knowingly making inaccurate or misleading statements in the transparency report is prohibited, with a good-faith exception (Sec. 111(d)).
 This is a discussion draft dated 2026-06-02, so these provisions may change.
 For questions about how these requirements apply to a specific organization, consulting qualified legal counsel is advisable.
 Sec. 111 Sec. 101 What is a large frontier developer under the bill?
 Under the draft bill, a "large frontier developer" is defined in Sec. 101 as a frontier developer that, in the calendar year immediately before the year at issue, had more than $500,000,000 in gross revenue — counting revenue collectively with every affiliate of that developer.
 To break that down, it builds on two earlier definitions:
 A "frontier developer" is an entity that has trained (or initiated the training of) a frontier model AND had more than $50,000,000 in gross revenue (with affiliates) in the preceding calendar year. (Sec. 101)
 A "frontier model" is a foundation model trained using more than 10²⁶ integer or floating-point operations, including the original training run and any subsequent fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or other substantial modification the developer applies to it. (Sec. 101)
 So, in plain terms, a large frontier developer is a company (or similar entity) that:
 1. Has trained a very large AI model (above the 10²⁶ compute threshold), and
 2. Brought in more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior year, counting affiliated entities together.
 This distinction matters because the draft imposes the most significant obligations — such as publishing a frontier AI framework (Sec. 111) and undergoing semi-annual independent audits (Sec. 112) — specifically on large frontier developers.

# Section-by-Section Summary 

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (Discussion Draft) 

Section 1. Short title; table of contents. 

Establishes the short title of the bill as the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act and provides the table of contents. 

# TITLE I — FRONTIER ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE GOVERNANCE 

Subtitle A — Definitions and the Center for AI Standards and Innovation Sec. 101. Definitions. 

Defines key terms used throughout the Act, including acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation, artificial intelligence, artificial intelligence models, catastrophic risk, critical safety incident, foundation model, frontier AI framework, frontier developer, frontier model, independent verification organization (IVO), large frontier developer, material modification, model weight, and substantial modification. 

Sec. 102. Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI). 

Formally establishes CAISI within the Department of Commerce, directed by a Secretary appointed Director. CAISI will develop voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security (adversarial robustness, interpretability, supply chain threats, model tampering, etc.), evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress, support synthetic content detection tools, and administer the IVO licensing regime. $100 million per year authorized for 2027–2029, with additional fee authority from IVOs and large frontier developers. Grants special authorities for CAISI to hire critical technical experts and fix their pay at levels above the GS scale. 

Subtitle B — Transparency, Independent Verification, and Whistleblower Protections Sec. 111. Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence. 

Large frontier developers (>$500M in revenue) must write, implement, comply with, and publicly post a frontier AI framework covering risk thresholds and assessment procedures for catastrophic risk, model weight cybersecurity, and both internal and external deployment decisions. Before, or concurrently with, deploying any new frontier model, frontier developers must publish a report disclosing the release date, supported languages, output modalities, intended use, restrictions, risk assessments, and mitigation steps. Redactions are permitted to protect trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety, or national security. Additionally, developers must file a report with CAISI within 15 days of a critical safety incident or within 24 hours if the incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. State attorneys general may also opt to receive such reports. Violations can result in fines of up to $1M per day, and the federal and state AGs can seek injunctions. Sec. 112. Independent Verification Organization (IVO) Audits and Assessments. 

CAISI licenses IVOs to audit large frontier developers' compliance with Secs. 111 and to assess whether developers' AI frameworks achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation. Licenses may be revoked for material failures of independence, obsolete methods, or non-compliance. Large frontier developers must retain a licensed IVO to verify compliance with their framework and to ensure the adequacy of the framework and procedures. These IVOs must be granted sufficient access to company materials, and report their audits to CAISI. IVOs are immune from claims of loss from an AI model they have audited. State AGs may opt into receiving all audit and assessment reports from IVOs. IVOs may refer violations of this section to the AG, or to state AGs who have opted into receiving such referrals. 

Sec. 113. Anti-Retaliation Protection for AI Whistleblowers. 

Prohibits AI companies from discriminating or retaliating in any way against employees or independent contractors for lawfully reporting a violation of federal AI law. If violated, employees are entitled to reinstatement, two times back pay with interest, compensatory damages, litigation costs, and attorney's fees. 

Subtitle C — Federalization and Federal Resources Sec. 121. Federalization of State Laws Regulating AI Model Development. 

Preempts any state or local law or regulation specifically targeting the development of AI models. Expressly does not preempt laws of general applicability, common law remedies, or laws regulating AI use or deployment. Sunsets three years post-enactment. 

Sec. 122. GAO Report on Regulatory Impediments to AI Innovation. 

Requires the Comptroller General to submit a report identifying federal statutes and regulations that directly affect AI innovation or unduly burden AI infrastructure (including energy), evaluating federal AI adoption progress, and providing legislative and administrative recommendations. 

Sec. 123. Resources for AI Model Documentation. 

NIST must establish a pilot program to create a template for documenting AI models and associated data (covering model name, developer identity, release date, training data cutoff, supported languages, terms of service, etc.), with technical guidelines and objective performance metrics. 

Subtitle D — AI Fraud Deterrence Sec. 131. Financial Crimes and Artificial Intelligence. 

Amends the federal mail fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, and money laundering statutes to increase maximum fines from $1 million to $2 million and increase penalties when AI is used. 

Sec. 132. AI Impersonation of Federal Officials. Adds penalties when AI is used to impersonate government officials. 

Subtitle E — Free Speech Sec. 141. Preventing Censorship and Protecting Free Speech. 

Directs the Secretary of Commerce to conduct a study examining how the government encourages or pressures AI companies with respect to content moderation or limiting of expression. The report must include recommendations for legislation providing individuals redress against unlawful government censorship of AI platforms, including transparency requirements and oversight mechanisms. 

TITLE II — WORKFORCE Subtitle A — AI Education and Capacity Building Sec. 201. AI Literacy Efforts of the AI Task Force. Directs the NSF Director to support the National STEM Teacher Corps pilot and Computer Science for All programs, consistent with recommendations of the House AI Task Force. 

Sec. 211. Preparing K–12 Educators and Students for an AI-Literate Future. Authorizes NSF to make competitive grants to universities and nonprofits for research on AI literacy curriculum, educator professional development, and evaluation tools for K–12 AI literacy. 

Sec. 221. Expanding Capacity in Artificial Intelligence Science. Directs NSF to establish a grant program for institutions not among the top 100 in federal R&D expenditures to broaden participation in AI research

Section-by-Section Summary 

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (Discussion Draft) 

Section 1. Short title; table of contents. 

Establishes the short title of the bill as the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act and provides the table of contents. 

# TITLE I — FRONTIER ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE GOVERNANCE 

Subtitle A — Definitions and the Center for AI Standards and Innovation 

Sec. 101. Definitions. 

Defines key terms used throughout the Act, including acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation, artificial intelligence, artificial intelligence models, catastrophic risk, critical safety incident, foundation model, frontier AI framework, frontier developer, frontier model, independent verification organization (IVO), large frontier developer, material modification, model weight, and substantial modification. 

Sec. 102. Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI). 

Formally establishes CAISI within the Department of Commerce, directed by a Secretary appointed Director. CAISI will develop voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security (adversarial robustness, interpretability, supply chain threats, model tampering, etc.), evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress, support synthetic content detection tools, and administer the IVO licensing regime. $100 million per year authorized for 2027 –2029, with additional fee authority from IVOs and large frontier developers. Grants special authorities for CAISI to hire critical technical experts and fix their pay at levels above the GS scale. 

Subtitle B — Transparency, Independent Verification, and Whistleblower Protections 

Sec. 111. Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence. 

Large frontier developers (>$500M in revenue) must write, implement, comply with, and publicly post a frontier AI framework covering risk thresholds and assessment procedures for catastrophic risk, model weight cybersecurity, and both internal and external deployment decisions. Before, or concurrently with, deploying any new frontier model, frontier developers must publish a report disclosing the release date, supported languages, output modalities, intended use, restrictions, risk assessments, and mitigation steps. Redactions are permitted to protect trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety, or national security. Additionally, developers must file a report with CAISI within 15 days of a critical safety incident or within 24 hours if the incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. State attorneys general may also opt to receive such reports. Violations can result in fines of up to $1M per day, and the federal and state AGs can seek injunctions. Sec. 112. Independent Verification Organization (IVO) Audits and Assessments. 

CAISI licenses IVOs to audit large frontier developers' compliance with Secs. 111 and to assess whether developers' AI frameworks achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation. Licenses may be revoked for material failures of independence, obsolete methods, or non-compliance. Large frontier developers must retain a licensed IVO to verify compliance with their framework and to ensure the adequacy of the framework and procedures. These IVOs must be granted sufficient access to company materials, and report their audits to CAISI. IVOs are immune from claims of loss from an AI model they have audited. State AGs may opt into receiving all audit and assessment reports from IVOs. IVOs may refer violations of this section to the AG, or to state AGs who have opted into receiving such referrals. 

Sec. 113. Anti-Retaliation Protection for AI Whistleblowers. 

Prohibits AI companies from discriminating or retaliating in any way against employees or independent contractors for lawfully reporting a violation of federal AI law. If violated, employees are entitled to reinstatement, two times back pay with interest, compensatory damages, litigation costs, and attorney's fees. 

Subtitle C — Federalization and Federal Resources 

Sec. 121. Federalization of State Laws Regulating AI Model Development. 

Preempts any state or local law or regulation specifically targeting the development of AI models. Expressly does not preempt laws of general applicability, common law remedies, or laws regulating AI use or deployment. Sunsets three years post-enactment. 

Sec. 122. GAO Report on Regulatory Impediments to AI Innovation. 

Requires the Comptroller General to submit a report identifying federal statutes and regulations that directly affect AI innovation or unduly burden AI infrastructure (including energy), evaluating federal AI adoption progress, and providing legislative and administrative recommendations. 

Sec. 123. Resources for AI Model Documentation. 

NIST must establish a pilot program to create a template for documenting AI models and associated data (covering model name, developer identity, release date, training data cutoff, supported languages, terms of service, etc.), with technical guidelines and objective performance metrics. 

Subtitle D — AI Fraud Deterrence 

Sec. 131. Financial Crimes and Artificial Intelligence. 

Amends the federal mail fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, and money laundering statutes to increase maximum fines from $1 million to $2 million and increase penalties when AI is used. 

Sec. 132. AI Impersonation of Federal Officials. Adds penalties when AI is used to impersonate government officials. 

Subtitle E — Free Speech 

Sec. 141. Preventing Censorship and Protecting Free Speech. 

Directs the Secretary of Commerce to conduct a study examining how the government encourages or pressures AI companies with respect to content moderation or limiting of expression. The report must include recommendations for legislation providing individuals redress against unlawful government censorship of AI platforms, including transparency requirements and oversight mechanisms. 

TITLE II — WORKFORCE 

Subtitle A — AI Education and Capacity Building 

Sec. 201. AI Literacy Efforts of the AI Task Force. Directs the NSF Director to support the National STEM Teacher Corps pilot and Computer Science for All programs, consistent with recommendations of the House AI Task Force. 

Sec. 211. Preparing K –12 Educators and Students for an AI-Literate Future. Authorizes NSF to make competitive grants to universities and nonprofits for research on AI literacy curriculum, educator professional development, and evaluation tools for K –12 AI literacy. 

Sec. 221. Expanding Capacity in Artificial Intelligence Science. Directs NSF to establish a grant program for institutions not among the top 100 in federal R&D expenditures to broaden participation in AI research, education, and workforce development.

{"path":"/workspace/out/comment_letter_GAAIA.md","content":"# COMMENT LETTER - DRAFT FOR CEO SIGN-OFF (WORK ORDER ACIA-POL-2026-117)

October 23, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Committee on Energy and Commerce
Washington, DC 20515

Submitted via: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

Dear Representatives Obernolte and Trahan:

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) thanks you for producing a serious, bipartisan draft and for taking stakeholder comment before introduction. Our 140 members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads this technology or cedes it to Beijing. We write to support the parts of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act that get us to one national standard, and to be direct about the parts that do not.

We support Sec. 121, the preemption of state laws specifically regulating AI model development. We ask that it be made permanent. We oppose Sec. 111's mandatory incident reporting, Sec. 102's codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), and the independent verification organization regime in Sec. 112. Those provisions write unfounded loss-of-control scenarios into federal law, and they should be struck. We support most of Titles III and IV, including the testbed program in Sec. 401, the international standards coalitions in Sec. 411, and the National AI Research Resource codification in Sec. 423.

## 1. Make the preemption in Sec. 121 permanent

Sec. 121 is the most important provision in the draft. It preempts any state or local law or regulation specifically targeting the development of AI models, and it expressly preserves laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state laws regulating use or deployment. That architecture is right. Development is a national activity, and it cannot be carried out under 50 different sets of rules.

Our members feel the patchwork now. California's SB 53 took effect January 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act takes effect January 1, 2027. Illinois has already enacted a third variant. In an August 2026 survey of our members, 61% named conflicting state definitions as their single largest compliance problem, and 34% of surveyed startups reported delaying a launch in California or New York in the last 12 months because of state AI rules. Among developers above $500 million in revenue, the median cost of running a published frontier safety framework is $1.4 million a year, and the median compliance burden of SB 53 and RAISE in parallel is 6.5 full-time employees. That is what two states cost. A third and a fourth state do not make that linear.

Three years is not enough. The sunset in Sec. 121 does not buy certainty for a training run or a data-center buildout; both are multi-year commitments made before the sunset expires. A sunset also tells state legislatures that a patchwork clock is running, which invites exactly the activity the preemption is meant to stop. Congress should decide the question once. We ask the sponsors to strike the sunset and make Sec. 121 permanent, and to state clearly in report language that Sec. 121 reaches state frontier-development mandates, including framework-publication and incident-reporting duties attached to model development.

## 2. Strike mandatory incident reporting in Sec. 111

Sec. 111 requires frontier developers to file a critical safety incident report with CAISI within 15 days, or within 24 hours if there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury, with civil penalties up to $1 million per day and enforcement by federal and state attorneys general.

The problem is the definition. Under Sec. 101(7), a "critical safety incident" includes "loss of control" of a frontier model and "a frontier model using deceptive techniques against its frontier developer." Neither requires an injury to a human being. Compare SB 53, where the model-weights prong applies only if it "results in death or bodily injury." The federal definition is broader than the California one it is meant to replace, and it turns a speculative hypothesis into a reportable federal violation.

We do not accept the premise. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. The scenarios behind this provision come from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations, amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network. Dangerous-capability and "scheming" studies are lab setups that say nothing about real-world risk. Congress should not give that material the force of law, and it should not attach a $1 million per day penalty to it.

The reporting channel also creates a standing federal intelligence function that has no mandate elsewhere in the federal government. If a developer's systems cause death or bodily injury, existing criminal and civil law, product liability law, and the fraud and impersonation provisions in Secs. 131 and 132 already reach it. Mandatory reporting to a federal AI registry, on loss-of-control and deception triggers, is regulation in search of an incident.

We ask the sponsors to strike Sec. 111's incident-reporting requirements and the associated enforcement in Sec. 101(7) definitions and Sec. 111(g), along with the "critical safety incident" and "catastrophic risk" definitions in Sec. 101(6) and (7). If a federal reporting channel is retained at all, it should trigger on actual harm to identifiable people, defined to the same standard as the rest of the U.S. Code.

## 3. Strike the CAISI codification and the audit regime in Secs. 102 and 112

Sec. 102 codifies CAISI inside the Department of Commerce, gives it a $100 million annual authorization for fiscal 2027 through 2029, and tasks it with voluntary guidelines, testing of AI systems, monitoring of "AI progress," and administration of the independent verification organization (IVO) licensing regime in Sec. 112. Sec. 112 requires large frontier developers to retain a licensed IVO to verify compliance with their frameworks and to assess whether they achieve "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation."

We ask the sponsors to strike both. Three points.

First, this is a regulator built on an unfounded premise. The "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" standard in Sec. 101(1) cannot be measured, tested or verified, because the risks it describes do not occur. A federal bureau chartered to police them will spend a decade chasing nothing.

Second, it is a case study in regulatory capture. CAISI licenses the auditors, sets the standards those auditors certify against, and collects fees from the companies it regulates. The audited get to choose their auditor only from CAISI's list. That arrangement would not be tolerated in any other industry, and it should not be created here.

Third, it is duplicative. Congress does not need a new Commerce bureau to do this. NIST already has the mandate and the measurement-science expertise, and the fiscal 2026 joint explanatory statement directs at least $55 million to NIST's ongoing AI research and measurement science work. That is where this work belongs. We also ask appropriators not to fund the Sec. 102 authorization, and to return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.

## 4. What we support

We support and encourage the sponsors to strengthen:

- Sec. 121 preemption (make permanent).
- Sec. 122, the GAO report on regulatory impediments to AI innovation, including energy and infrastructure barriers.
- Sec. 123, the NIST model documentation pilot. Voluntary, standardized and industry-led is exactly the right design.
- Sec. 141, the study on government pressure on AI platforms' content decisions.
- Secs. 131 and 132, the fraud and impersonation provisions. Real harm, real remedies, existing criminal law.
- Sec. 311, CISA grants to critical open-source software maintainers, and Sec. 321, the report on model weight, data center and open-source security. Weight security is a real, demonstrated risk and we welcome the attention.
- Sec. 401, the testbed program. Our members will participate, and we would ask that testbed activities remain voluntary and that results not be treated as compliance findings.
- Sec. 411, international coalitions to counter foreign adversary influence in standards bodies. We support excluding China from the listed criteria and ask that industry be included in the delegations.
- Sec. 423, codifying the National AI Research Resource.

## Conclusion

The draft gets the most important thing right: it puts the federal government between 50 legislatures and American AI developers. That is where the federal government belongs. We ask you to keep that, make it permanent, and remove the parts of the bill that treat speculation as fact. ACIA members would rather comply with one national standard than twelve state ones, and they will support a bill that delivers one.

We appreciate the sponsors' openness, and Energy and Commerce's engagement on this. We are available to work with your staff, or with the committee, on technical language for the preemption, definitions and Title III provisions.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

# COMMENT LETTER - DRAFT FOR CEO SIGN-OFF (WORK ORDER ACIA-POL-2026-117)

**DO NOT SEND FROM THIS WORKSPACE. Route through President & CEO for signature, then to GAAIA@mail.house.gov.**

---

October 23, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Committee on Energy and Commerce
Washington, DC 20515

Submitted via: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

Dear Representatives Obernolte and Trahan:

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) thanks you for producing a serious, bipartisan draft and for taking stakeholder comment before introduction. Our 140 members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads this technology or cedes it to Beijing. We write to support the parts of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act that get us to one national standard, and to be direct about the parts that do not.

We support Sec. 121, the preemption of state laws specifically regulating AI model development. We ask that it be made permanent. We oppose Sec. 111's mandatory incident reporting, Sec. 102's codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), and the independent verification organization regime in Sec. 112. Those provisions write unfounded loss-of-control scenarios into federal law, and they should be struck. We support most of Titles III and IV, including the testbed program in Sec. 401, the international standards coalitions in Sec. 411, and the National AI Research Resource codification in Sec. 423.

## 1. Make the preemption in Sec. 121 permanent

Sec. 121 is the most important provision in the draft. It preempts any state or local law or regulation specifically targeting the development of AI models, and it expressly preserves laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state laws regulating use or deployment. That architecture is right. Development is a national activity, and it cannot be carried out under 50 different sets of rules.

Our members feel the patchwork now. California's SB 53 took effect January 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act takes effect January 1, 2027. Illinois has already enacted a third variant. In an August 2026 survey of our members, 61% named conflicting state definitions as their single largest compliance problem, and 34% of surveyed startups reported delaying a launch in California or New York in the last 12 months because of state AI rules. Among developers above $500 million in revenue, the median cost of running a published frontier safety framework is $1.4 million a year, and the median compliance burden of SB 53 and RAISE in parallel is 6.5 full-time employees. That is what two states cost. A third and a fourth state do not make that linear.

Three years is not enough. The sunset in Sec. 121 does not buy certainty for a training run or a data-center buildout; both are multi-year commitments made before the sunset expires. A sunset also tells state legislatures that a patchwork clock is running, which invites exactly the activity the preemption is meant to stop. Congress should decide the question once. We ask the sponsors to strike the sunset and make Sec. 121 permanent, and to state clearly in report language that Sec. 121 reaches state frontier-development mandates, including framework-publication and incident-reporting duties attached to model development.

## 2. Strike mandatory incident reporting in Sec. 111

Sec. 111 requires frontier developers to file a critical safety incident report with CAISI within 15 days, or within 24 hours if there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury, with civil penalties up to $1 million per day and enforcement by federal and state attorneys general.

The problem is the definition. Under Sec. 101(7), a "critical safety incident" includes "loss of control" of a frontier model and "a frontier model using deceptive techniques against its frontier developer." Neither requires an injury to a human being. Compare SB 53, where the model-weights prong applies only if it "results in death or bodily injury." The federal definition is broader than the California one it is meant to replace, and it turns a speculative hypothesis into a reportable federal violation.

We do not accept the premise. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. The scenarios behind this provision come from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations, amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network. Dangerous-capability and "scheming" studies are lab setups that say nothing about real-world risk. Congress should not give that material the force of law, and it should not attach a $1 million per day penalty to it.

The reporting channel also creates a standing federal intelligence function that has no mandate elsewhere in the federal government. If a developer's systems cause death or bodily injury, existing criminal and civil law, product liability law, and the fraud and impersonation provisions in Secs. 131 and 132 already reach it. Mandatory reporting to a federal AI registry, on loss-of-control and deception triggers, is regulation in search of an incident.

We ask the sponsors to strike Sec. 111's incident-reporting requirements and the associated enforcement in Sec. 101(7) definitions and Sec. 111(g), along with the "critical safety incident" and "catastrophic risk" definitions in Sec. 101(6) and (7). If a federal reporting channel is retained at all, it should trigger on actual harm to identifiable people, defined to the same standard as the rest of the U.S. Code.

## 3. Strike the CAISI codification and the audit regime in Secs. 102 and 112

Sec. 102 codifies CAISI inside the Department of Commerce, gives it a $100 million annual authorization for fiscal 2027 through 2029, and tasks it with voluntary guidelines, testing of AI systems, monitoring of "AI progress," and administration of the independent verification organization (IVO) licensing regime in Sec. 112. Sec. 112 requires large frontier developers to retain a licensed IVO to verify compliance with their frameworks and to assess whether they achieve "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation."

We ask the sponsors to strike both. Three points.

First, this is a regulator built on an unfounded premise. The "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" standard in Sec. 101(1) cannot be measured, tested or verified, because the risks it describes do not occur. A federal bureau chartered to police them will spend a decade chasing nothing.

Second, it is a case study in regulatory capture. CAISI licenses the auditors, sets the standards those auditors certify against, and collects fees from the companies it regulates. The audited get to choose their auditor only from CAISI's list. That arrangement would not be tolerated in any other industry, and it should not be created here.

Third, it is duplicative. Congress does not need a new Commerce bureau to do this. NIST already has the mandate and the measurement-science expertise, and the fiscal 2026 joint explanatory statement directs at least $55 million to NIST's ongoing AI research and measurement science work. That is where this work belongs. We also ask appropriators not to fund the Sec. 102 authorization, and to return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.

## 4. What we support

We support and encourage the sponsors to strengthen:

- Sec. 121 preemption (make permanent).
- Sec. 122, the GAO report on regulatory impediments to AI innovation, including energy and infrastructure barriers.
- Sec. 123, the NIST model documentation pilot. Voluntary, standardized and industry-led is exactly the right design.
- Sec. 141, the study on government pressure on AI platforms' content decisions.
- Secs. 131 and 132, the fraud and impersonation provisions. Real harm, real remedies, existing criminal law.
- Sec. 311, CISA grants to critical open-source software maintainers, and Sec. 321, the report on model weight, data center and open-source security. Weight security is a real, demonstrated risk and we welcome the attention.
- Sec. 401, the testbed program. Our members will participate, and we would ask that testbed activities remain voluntary and that results not be treated as compliance findings.
- Sec. 411, international coalitions to counter foreign adversary influence in standards bodies. We support excluding China from the listed criteria and ask that industry be included in the delegations.
- Sec. 423, codifying the National AI Research Resource.

## Conclusion

The draft gets the most important thing right: it puts the federal government between 50 legislatures and American AI developers. That is where the federal government belongs. We ask you to keep that, make it permanent, and remove the parts of the bill that treat speculation as fact. ACIA members would rather comply with one national standard than twelve state ones, and they will support a bill that delivers one.

We appreciate the sponsors' openness, and Energy and Commerce's engagement on this. We are available to work with your staff, or with the committee, on technical language for the preemption, definitions and Title III provisions.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

{"content": "# ACIA ONE-PAGER: GREAT AMERICAN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ACT (GAAIA) DISCUSSION DRAFT
**For House Energy & Commerce member offices | ACIA | Oct. 2026 | Draft, not for distribution**

## ONE NATIONAL STANDARD, NOT A FEDERAL PATCHWORK

ACIA is a Washington-based coalition of 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms. We support the GAAIA discussion draft's centerpiece: Sec. 121 preempts state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. We ask the committee to keep it, make it permanent, and cut the provisions that would build a federal regulator around risks that have never materialized.

### The problem in the states

- California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. Illinois has enacted a third variant.
- 61% of surveyed ACIA members name conflicting state definitions as their top compliance issue.
- 34% of surveyed member startups delayed a California or New York launch in the past 12 months because of state AI rules.
- Developers above $500 million in revenue report a median of 6.5 full-time employees just to comply with SB 53 and RAISE in parallel, and a median $1.4 million a year to maintain a published frontier safety framework.

### OUR FIVE ASKS

**1. Make Sec. 121 preemption permanent.** Strike the three-year sunset. Multi-year training runs and data-center builds need certainty, and a sunset invites the patchwork back.

**2. Close the state back doors.** Strike the state attorney general opt-ins in Secs. 111 and 112 for incident reports, audit reports and enforcement referrals. A federal law that files to 50 states on request is a patchwork with a federal letterhead.

**3. Strike mandatory incident reporting.** Sec. 111 requires filing within 15 days, or 24 hours for imminent risk, with penalties up to $1 million per day. The trigger definition in Sec. 101(7) includes "loss of control" and a model "using deceptive techniques" with no injury required. It is broader than SB 53. Mandates should attach to real harm, not speculative doomsday scenarios.

**4. Strike CAISI.** Sec. 102 codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation and authorizes $100 million a year for fiscal 2027-2029. NIST already has the measurement-science mission, with at least $55 million directed to AI work in fiscal 2026. A bureau that licenses its own auditors, sets their standards and charges fees to the companies it regulates is regulatory capture by design.

**5. Fund what works.** Keep Sec. 401 testbeds, Sec. 411 international standards coalitions, Sec. 311 open-source maintainer grants, Sec. 321 model-weight security review, Sec. 123 the voluntary NIST documentation pilot, and Sec. 423 NAIRR codification. Industry will participate if participation stays voluntary.

### BOTTOM LINE

The federal government belongs between 50 state legislatures and American AI builders. Keep that, make it permanent, and cut the parts that write speculation into the U.S. Code.

**Contact:** ACIA policy team | GAAIA comment letter filed to GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**ACIA member newsletter | ~150 words | Draft for review**

## ACIA files comments on the Great American AI Act draft

On Oct. 23, ACIA filed comments with Reps. Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan on their Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft.

Our bottom line is simple. We support Sec. 121, which preempts state laws that specifically regulate AI model development, and we asked the sponsors to strike the three-year sunset so it becomes permanent. California's SB 53 is already in effect and New York's RAISE Act follows in January, so one national standard matters to every member building or deploying models.

We asked the sponsors to strike three things: mandatory incident reporting keyed to "loss of control" and model "deception," the codification of CAISI and its $100 million annual authorization, and the CAISI-licensed auditor regime. We backed the testbed program, international standards coalitions, open-source maintainer grants and NAIRR codification.

Your aggregate survey data made the case. Thank you to the 86 members who responded.

{"content": "# STAFF Q&A - GAAIA DISCUSSION DRAFT
**Work order ACIA-POL-2026-117 | Answers for ACIA staff in Hill meetings | Draft, not for external distribution | Each answer 120 words or fewer**

## Q1. (Majority E&C staff) "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."

Preemption and reporting answer different questions. Preemption is about who gets to set the rule. Reporting is about whether the substance is justified, and this substance is not. Worse, the draft is not lighter than SB 53. California's law triggers its model-weights prong only on "death or bodily injury." Sec. 101(7) of the draft triggers on any unauthorized access to model weights, on "loss of control," and on a model "using deceptive techniques against its frontier developer," all with no injury requirement. Add a $1 million per day federal penalty and state AG opt-in, and the federal version reaches further than the state one it displaces. We will take the jurisdictional fix and pass on the mandate.

## Q2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"

Several, and the draft already contains them. We support the fraud and AI impersonation provisions in Secs. 131 and 132, the model-weight and data-center security review in Sec. 321, open-source maintainer support in Sec. 311, and the testbed program in Sec. 401, which our members will use. We also accept mandatory reporting where a real person is actually harmed, through the agencies Congress already trusts: DOJ, FTC and CISA. What we do not accept is pre-emptive federal reporting keyed to "loss of control" and model "deception." Those triggers come from contrived lab setups and speculative doomsday scenarios, not from any harm that has occurred. Members take security obligations seriously, which is exactly why we want them drafted around real risks.

## Q3. (Senate Commerce staff) "Three years or permanent? What's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"

Permanent. No sunset, no reauthorization trigger, no study-and-report clause that becomes a reopening vehicle. Two reasons. First, the planning horizon problem: training runs, fab commitments and data-center buildouts are made three to five years out, so a three-year fuse adds no certainty at all. Second, the incentive problem: a sunset tells every state legislature and every interest group that the patchwork clock is running, which invites precisely the activity preemption exists to stop. Congress should decide the question once. The right model is not a moratorium. It is a decision.

## Q4. (Appropriations staff) "CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?"

Zero, and the authorization should be struck along with it. This is not a level question. CAISI is chartered to police "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," a standard that cannot be measured because the underlying risks have never materialized. It would also license its own auditors, set the standards those auditors certify against and charge fees to the companies it regulates. That is regulatory capture by design. The sponsors' own FAQ puts current CAISI funding around $15 million, so this is a roughly tenfold expansion. NIST already holds the measurement-science mission, with at least $55 million directed to AI work in fiscal 2026. Fund NIST. Fund the testbeds and NAIRR. Do not fund CAISI.

 On June 4, US Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) released a discussion draft of the bipartisan Great American AI Act of 2026 ( GAAIA ), which would establish a framework regulating artificial intelligence ( AI ) at the federal level.

 On 

 The  draft builds upon work from the bipartisan House AI Task Force. Representatives Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.), Scott Franklin (R-Fla.), Scott Peters (D-Calif.), and Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) joined in releasing the draft.
 Many observers believe that the current Obernolte-Trahan discussion draft bill is unlikely to pass out of committee or the House based on opposition from some in industry and various Members of Congress, including the leaders of the House Democrat AI Task Force. It may be best to view this new bipartisan bill as a conversation starter developed because of frustration that Congress has not yet really legislated on AI. The draft bill has been thrust into a complicated tech policy arena that includes many interconnected issues. Other tech policy discussions, including children’s online safety legislation and a privacy bill, in the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce Committee’s potential consideration of legislation impacting AI chatbots, children’s online safety, or a social media ban for some children could all be lumped in with various AI initiatives from the White House to attract additional support. Every few days, there are new developments in the AI policy area within the Administration and Congress, but it is helpful to see where Reps. Obernolte and Trahan were able to identify bipartisan consensus.
 Objectives of the GAAIA 
 The 269-page  draft would establish a federal AI governance regime addressing national security, cybersecurity, workforce, and innovation. If enacted, the legislation would create a framework for frontier-model oversight, codify the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), expand federal attention to workforce and labor-market effects, review federal AI adoption and related regulatory barriers, address government “jawboning” of AI platforms, advance AI research, development, and international cooperation, and temporarily preempt state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. The research and international-cooperation provisions include support for AI testbeds, codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), and limits on the People’s Republic of China’s participation in US-led standards coalitions. The draft follows President Trump’s June 2 executive order establishing voluntary federal agency reviews of frontier AI models and the White House’s March National Policy Framework for AI, which called on US Congress to preempt state AI laws imposing “undue burdens.”
 Frontier Model Oversight and Incident Reporting 
 The GAAIA would establish a federal oversight framework for advanced AI developers that fall into one of two categories: “frontier developer,” which is any entity that has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier model and that, collectively with its affiliates, had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year, and “large frontier developer,” which is an entity that meets the same test but had more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year. The distinction matters because some obligations — such as transparency reports and critical-safety incident reporting — would apply to all frontier developers, while others — such as the published frontier AI framework and the independent audit regime — apply only to large frontier developers. The GAAIA distinguishes between general AI deployment and the development of frontier systems, with preemption and oversight provisions focused on the development side. Notably, the frontier transparency and audit requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would themselves sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them.
 Frontier AI Framework:  The GAAIA would require each large frontier developer to write, implement, comply with, and clearly and conspicuously publish on a publicly available website a “frontier AI framework” — technical and organizational protocols to assess, mitigate, and manage catastrophic risk — within one year of enactment, and to review and update that framework at least annually.

 Reporting Obligations:  The GAAIA would require frontier developers to report certain “critical safety incidents” — defined as unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model’s weights; a failure of the model’s risk-mitigation measures; or loss of control of the model — to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury.

 Review and Audit Requirements:  Large frontier developers would be required to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization (IVO) to perform audits and assessments at least semi-annually and, on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI director’s request, grant the IVO timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel, and systems, and submit post-audit reports. The IVO would assess not only the large frontier developer’s compliance with the law, but also whether the developer’s frontier AI framework is adequate to achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation.

 Whistleblower Protections 
 The GAAIA would also protect AI whistleblowers from retaliation. These protections could not be waived or altered by contract, including by any pre-dispute arbitration or other alternative-dispute-resolution agreement, and available remedies include double back pay with interest and compensatory damages such as litigation costs, expert witness fees, and reasonable attorneys’ fees.
 Codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation 
 The GAAIA would codify CAISI within the US Department of Commerce and place it at the center of the legislation’s federal standards and evaluation framework. Key obligations for CAISI under the GAIAA include: 
 Developing voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security and related evaluation work.

 Evaluating and monitoring activities tied to advanced AI systems.

 Supporting synthetic content detection tools.

 Administering the licensing regime for independent verification organizations that audit large frontier developers.

 Key provisions on AI transparency, audits, and federal preemption Written by : Tony Samp Danny Tobey Ashley Carr Alicia Smith Michael Atleson On June 4, 2026, Representative Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of artificial intelligence (AI) legislation titled the “Great American AI Act” (GAAIA). The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint op-ed in Bloomberg Law .

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and preemption: “Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough.”

 AI’s impact on the workforce: “Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.”

 US leadership internationally: “By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.”

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

 While several members have joined in supporting the discussion draft , including Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Scott Peters (D-CA), the House Democratic Commission on AI came out in opposition hours after release of the draft text.

 The draft legislation spans 269 pages and contains titles devoted to:

 Frontier AI Government (Title I)

 Workforce (Title II)

 Cybersecurity (Title III)

 Research, Development, and International Cooperation (Title IV)

 Transparency in frontier AI models 

 The bill contains provisions that would require developers of frontier AI models to disclose information about those models (Section 111), obtain a form of third-party audit (Section 112), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers (Section 113).

 Section 111 

 Section 111 would require large frontier AI model developers to publish a “frontier AI framework” focused on risk mitigation and the handling of “catastrophic risk.” All frontier model developers would be required to publish transparency reports containing additional information and submit reports of any “critical safety incidents” to the Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence Standards and Innovation (CAISI).

 Section 112 

 Section 112 would create a federal system in which the CAISI Director would license and oversee “independent verification organizations (IVOs)” that large frontier model developers would have to retain to perform “audits and assessments.”

 The IVOs would verify developer compliance with the law and assess the adequacy of the developer’s “frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks.”

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General (AG) and state AGs. Such referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both Sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 Section 113 

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding “AI violations.” This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations “related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence.”

 Similarities to other recently enacted bills 

 All three sections borrow heavily from recently enacted frontier model laws in California and New York , as well as a similar Illinois law that Governor JB Pritzker is expected to sign soon. The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is thus the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

 Another recently enacted state law in Virginia focuses on IVOs but imposes no requirements, instead directing state officials to evaluate the feasibility and impact of an IVO framework.

 Notable preemption provisions 

 Title I of the bill would preempt state laws and rules “specifically regulating the development of” any AI model, where “development” is broadly defined as “acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment.” The bill explains that the purpose of such preemption is to allow the federal government to “establish testing, evaluation, and oversight frameworks.” Such preemption would last for three years unless reauthorized.

 The bill makes clear that it does not apply post-deployment or preempt state laws or rules of "general applicability." Thus, many AI-related state bills and laws would remain unaffected, such as laws regulating companion bots  and commercial chatbot interactions .

 However, the preemption language could preempt several state laws imposing obligations on developers, including the three frontier developer laws described above.

 The draft text incorporates provisions from several bipartisan bills on AI policy addressing a variety of issues, including cybersecurity, AI education and workforce, fraud deterrence, whistleblower protections, data center energy efficiencies, and others.

# COMMENT LETTER - DRAFT FOR CEO SIGN-OFF (WORK ORDER ACIA-POL-2026-117)

**DO NOT SEND FROM THIS WORKSPACE. Route through President & CEO for signature, then to GAAIA@mail.house.gov.**

---

October 23, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Committee on Energy and Commerce
Washington, DC 20515

Submitted via: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

Dear Representatives Obernolte and Trahan:

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) thanks you for producing a serious, bipartisan draft and for taking stakeholder comment before introduction. Our 140 members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads this technology or cedes it to Beijing. We write to support the parts of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act that get us to one national standard, and to be direct about the parts that do not.

We support Sec. 121, the preemption of state laws specifically regulating AI model development. We ask that it be made permanent. We oppose Sec. 111's mandatory incident reporting, Sec. 102's codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), and the independent verification organization regime in Sec. 112. Those provisions write unfounded loss-of-control scenarios into federal law, and they should be struck. We support most of Titles III and IV, including the testbed program in Sec. 401, the international standards coalitions in Sec. 411, and the National AI Research Resource codification in Sec. 423.

## 1. Make the preemption in Sec. 121 permanent

Sec. 121 is the most important provision in the draft. It preempts any state or local law or regulation specifically targeting the development of AI models, and it expressly preserves laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state laws regulating use or deployment. That architecture is right. Development is a national activity, and it cannot be carried out under 50 different sets of rules.

Our members feel the patchwork now. California's SB 53 took effect January 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act takes effect January 1, 2027. Illinois followed on July 6, 2026, and takes effect January 1, 2027. In an August 2026 survey of our members, 61% named conflicting state definitions as their single largest compliance problem, and 34% of surveyed startups reported delaying a launch in California or New York in the last 12 months because of state AI rules. Among developers above $500 million in revenue, the median cost of running a published frontier safety framework is $1.4 million a year, and the median compliance burden of SB 53 and RAISE in parallel is 6.5 full-time employees. That is what two states cost. A third and a fourth state do not make that linear.

Preemption is also incomplete while Sec. 111 lets state attorneys general opt in to receive incident reports and Sec. 112 lets them opt in to receive audit reports and violation referrals. A federal standard that routes filings to 50 state enforcers on request is not one national standard. It is a patchwork with a federal letterhead. We ask the sponsors to remove those state opt-in back doors and put enforcement exclusively with the federal government.

Finally, the three-year sunset in Sec. 121 does not buy certainty for a training run or a data-center buildout; both are multi-year commitments made before the sunset expires. A sunset also tells state legislatures that a patchwork clock is running, which invites exactly the activity the preemption is meant to stop. Congress should decide the question once. We ask the sponsors to strike the sunset and make Sec. 121 permanent, and to state clearly in report language that Sec. 121 reaches state frontier-development mandates, including framework-publication and incident-reporting duties attached to model development.

## 2. Strike mandatory incident reporting in Sec. 111

Sec. 111 requires frontier developers to file a critical safety incident report with CAISI within 15 days, or within 24 hours if there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury, with civil penalties up to $1 million per day and enforcement by federal and state attorneys general.

The problem is the definition. Sec. 101(7) defines a "critical safety incident" as any of three things: unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of model weights; "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures"; or "loss of control of such model." Not one of the three requires an injury to a human being. Compare SB 53, where the model-weights prong applies only if it "results in death or bodily injury." The federal definition is broader than the California law it is meant to replace, and it turns a speculative hypothesis into a reportable federal violation. Under prong (B), a control that fails and harms no one is still a federal event.

We do not accept the premise. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. The scenarios behind this provision come from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations, amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network. Dangerous-capability and "scheming" studies are lab setups that say nothing about real-world risk. Congress should not give that material the force of law, and it should not attach a $1 million per day penalty to it.

The reporting channel also creates a standing federal intelligence function that has no mandate elsewhere in the federal government. If a developer's systems cause death or bodily injury, existing criminal and civil law, product liability law, and the fraud and impersonation provisions in Secs. 131 and 132 already reach it. Mandatory reporting to a federal AI registry, on triggers that require no injury, is regulation in search of an incident.

## 2a. The costs of a second reporting regime

Compliance costs are not hypothetical for our members. Building a federal reporting function on top of California's is not free. In our August 2026 survey, the median one-off cost of standing up an incident-reporting function was $310,000, with an interquartile range of $140,000 to $720,000, across 38 responding developers. For developers above $500 million in revenue, the median cost of maintaining a published frontier safety framework is $1.4 million a year, with an interquartile range of $800,000 to $2.6 million. Adding a federal filing, with a federal penalty of $1 million per day, on top of SB 53's Cal OES channel and RAISE's 72-hour clock, buys no additional safety. It buys three legal reviews of the same event.

We ask the sponsors to strike Sec. 111's incident-reporting requirements and the associated enforcement in Sec. 101(7) and Sec. 111(g), along with the "critical safety incident" and "catastrophic risk" definitions in Sec. 101(6) and (7). We also note that Secs. 111 and 112 sunset on the same three-year clock as Sec. 121. If Congress will not strike the mandates, it should at minimum decouple the two sunsets, so that a future reauthorization fight cannot be used to restore a patchwork. If a federal reporting channel is retained at all, it should trigger on actual harm to identifiable people, defined to the same standard as the rest of the U.S. Code.

## 3. Strike the CAISI codification and the audit regime in Secs. 102 and 112

Sec. 102 codifies CAISI inside the Department of Commerce, gives it a $100 million annual authorization for fiscal 2027 through 2029, and tasks it with voluntary guidelines, testing of AI systems, monitoring of "AI progress," and administration of the independent verification organization (IVO) licensing regime in Sec. 112. Sec. 112 requires large frontier developers to retain a licensed IVO to verify compliance with their frameworks and to assess whether they achieve "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation."

We ask the sponsors to strike both. Three points.

First, this is a regulator built on an unfounded premise. The "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" standard in Sec. 101(1) cannot be measured, tested or verified, because the risks it describes do not occur. A federal bureau chartered to police them will spend a decade chasing nothing.

Second, it is a case study in regulatory capture. CAISI licenses the auditors, sets the standards those auditors certify against, and collects fees from the companies it regulates. The audited get to choose their auditor only from CAISI's list. That arrangement would not be tolerated in any other industry, and it should not be created here.

Third, it is duplicative, and it is priced like a startup rather than a standards body. The $100 million annual authorization for fiscal 2027 through 2029 is roughly an order of magnitude above CAISI's current-year funding, per the sponsors' own FAQ, and it comes on top of fee authority charged to the companies being regulated and special authority to hire above the GS scale. Congress does not need a new Commerce bureau to do this. NIST already has the mandate and the measurement-science expertise, and the fiscal 2026 joint explanatory statement directs at least $55 million to NIST's ongoing AI research and measurement science work. That is where this work belongs. We also ask appropriators not to fund the Sec. 102 authorization, and to return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.

## 4. What we support

We support and encourage the sponsors to strengthen:

- Sec. 121 preemption (make permanent).
- Sec. 122, the GAO report on regulatory impediments to AI innovation, including energy and infrastructure barriers.
- Sec. 123, the NIST model documentation pilot. Voluntary, standardized and industry-led is exactly the right design.
- Sec. 141, the study on government pressure on AI platforms' content decisions.
- Secs. 131 and 132, the fraud and impersonation provisions. Real harm, real remedies, existing criminal law.
- Sec. 311, CISA grants to critical open-source software maintainers, and Sec. 321, the report on model weight, data center and open-source security. Weight security is a real, demonstrated risk and we welcome the attention.
- Sec. 401, the testbed program. Our members will participate, and we would ask that testbed activities remain voluntary and that results not be treated as compliance findings.
- Sec. 411, international coalitions to counter foreign adversary influence in standards bodies. We support excluding China from the listed criteria and ask that industry be included in the delegations.
- Sec. 423, codifying the National AI Research Resource.

## Conclusion

The draft gets the most important thing right: it puts the federal government between 50 legislatures and American AI developers. That is where the federal government belongs. We ask you to keep that, make it permanent, and remove the parts of the bill that treat speculation as fact. ACIA members would rather comply with one national standard than twelve state ones, and they will support a bill that delivers one.

We appreciate the sponsors' openness, and Energy and Commerce's engagement on this. We are available to work with your staff, or with the committee, on technical language for the preemption, definitions and Title III provisions.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
